items.title: "Error reading the log directory/files" always fires the first time
items.body:
## Bug Report

### Version

0.2.5

### Platform

All

### Crates

tracing-appender

### Description

The error `Error reading the log directory/files: No such file or directory (os error 2)` is always printed on first use, when the log directory doesn't exist yet.

This happens when using the [`RollingFileAppender`](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing/blob/d9d4c542de10f5d3a711b7a45ffe450fd0666437/tracing-appender/src/rolling.rs#L87) with [`max_files`](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing/blob/d9d4c542de10f5d3a711b7a45ffe450fd0666437/tracing-appender/src/rolling.rs#L112) set, because [`prune_old_logs`](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing/blob/d9d4c542de10f5d3a711b7a45ffe450fd0666437/tracing-appender/src/rolling.rs#L655) is [called when `max_files` has a value](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing/blob/d9d4c542de10f5d3a711b7a45ffe450fd0666437/tracing-appender/src/rolling.rs#L616), without taking into account if this is the first or nth time that gets executed.

The following snippet should help reproducing the error.

```rust
let file_appender = RollingFileAppender::builder()
        .rotation(Rotation::DAILY)
        .max_log_files(1)
        .filename_suffix("suffix".to_string())
        .build("some_folder");
```

I would expect this error not to appear for the first time, given that the folders won't exist. A possible solution would be to not send any message to `stderr` when the folder doesn't exist. That means the error would never appear when the folder doesn't exist. Doesn't mind if it's the 1st or nth execution.

The h2 crate, used internally by hyper, had a flaw that would accept and queue empty DATA frames without limit.
If streams were not actively drained, this could lead to unbounded memory usage, or a panic if the length overflows.

Low severity.

Patched in v0.4.16.

items.title: tracing-appender has broken symlinks when a relative path is specified
items.body:
## Bug Report

### Version

```
│   ├── tracing v0.1.44
│   │   ├── tracing-attributes v0.1.31 (proc-macro)
│   │   └── tracing-core v0.1.36
│   ├── tracing-appender v0.2.5
│   │   └── tracing-subscriber v0.3.23
│   │       ├── tracing-core v0.1.36 (*)
│   │       └── tracing-log v0.2.0
│   │           └── tracing-core v0.1.36 (*)
│   └── tracing-subscriber v0.3.23 (*)
└── tracing v0.1.44 (*)
```

### Platform

Linux 7.1.8-1-cachyos SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC x86_64 GNU/Linux

### Crates

tracing-appender v0.2.5

### Description

When using the `latest_symlink` feature added in #3447, if a *relative* path is specified to [`Builder::build`](https://docs.rs/tracing-appender/0.2.5/tracing_appender/rolling/struct.Builder.html#method.build), the symlink also uses the relative path. This results in broken symlinks when a relative path to a directory is specified.

For example, this code:
```rs
let appender = RollingFileAppender::builder()
    .rotation(Rotation::DAILY)
    .filename_prefix("myapp.log")
    .latest_symlink("latest.log")
    .build("./logs")
    .expect("failed to initialize rolling file appender");
```
Results in the symlink `latest.log` to point to `./logs/myapp.log.2019-01-01` while itself already *inside* of the `logs` directory, so it actually points to `./logs/./logs/myapp.log.2019-01-01`, which is invalid.

The workaround is to always specify an absolute path to `Builder::build`. But this should be fixed by providing the correct `path` to `symlink::symlink_file` (either absolute, or fixing the relative path so it's correct):
https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing/blob/d9d4c542de10f5d3a711b7a45ffe450fd0666437/tracing-appender/src/rolling.rs#L802-L808

## Bug Report

When `#[instrument]` is applied to a function, clippy no longer picks up uses of `eprintln!`, `eprint!`, `println!`, `print!` when linting for `clippy::print_stderr` or `clippy::print_stdout`, respectively.

The workaround I am using is to do `#[cfg_attr(not(clippy), instrument)]`, however this is not ideal.

In this [Rust Playground](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2024&gist=602f6152581b38847847680d83645a62) pick `Tools > Clippy` for an example of the bug, and the workaround.

items.title: Allow pass non-static level for `event!`
items.body:
## Feature Request

### Crates

<!--
If known, please specify the tracing crate or crates the new feature should
be added to. Otherwise, delete this section.
-->
* `tracing`

### Motivation

<!--
Please describe the use case(s) or other motivation for the new feature.
-->

Define in runtime, which event level is needed without external match. At the moment in such cases it lead to long and complex `match` or `if` expression, which lead to copy-paste errors.

The only thing which makes it impossible to use  is `static __CALLSITE` creation: `static __CALLSITE: $crate::callsite::DefaultCallsite = $crate::callsite2!` at `tracing-0.1.44/src/macros.rs:885:9`.

Additional motivation: https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing/issues/3585

### Proposal

<!--
How should the new feature be implemented, and why? Add any considered
drawbacks.
-->

in outer level: 

```rust
let t_level: tracing::Level = app_level.into();

tracing::event!(t_level, {field = %value}) // see example below for the main reasoning.
```

### Alternatives

<!--
Are there other ways to solve this problem that you've considered? What are
their potential drawbacks? Why was the proposed solution chosen over these
alternatives?
-->

One can use long copy-paste error-prone match case as shown below. there's no possibility to pass other parameters either to reduce maintenance burden, as most of them are part of the same static `__CALLSITE` expression.

```rust
/// Return app level for specific event.
fn obtain_level(/*...*/) -> app::Level { app:Level::Error };

// ...
match obtain_level() {
    Level::Error => tracing::event!(tracing::Level::ERROR, {field = %value}), // could be quite complex expression
    Level::Warn => tracing::event!(tracing::Level::WARN, {field = %value}), // copy-paste
    Level::Info => tracing::event!(tracing::Level::INFO, {field = %value}), // copy-paste
    Level::Debug => tracing::event!(tracing::Level::DEBUG, {field = %value}), // copy-paste
    Level::Trace => tracing::event!(tracing::Level::TRACE, {field = %value}), // copy-paste
}
```

items.title: fmt writer: allow to make a writer based on dynamic values
items.body:
The patch https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing/commit/805eb51bc9f5ab7d193c9f7b3f382526fd5dbf62 explains the motivation for the `MakeWriter::make_writer_for` method. However, this method only receives static metadata, which may not be sufficient in some cases.

For example, consider a server that accepts client connections and needs to write trace events for each connection to a separate file. The client IP address would likely be recorded as an event field rather than as the target, since dynamic targets are not supported (see #3178). Therefore, it would be useful to configure the writer based on dynamic field values.

Is there an existing workaround for this use case (of course, we can write a custom `Layer`, but it seems overkill)? If so, I would appreciate any guidance.

items.title: RUSTSEC-2026-0195: Unbounded namespace-declaration allocation in `NsReader` enables memory-exhaustion denial of service
items.body:
> Unbounded namespace-declaration allocation in `NsReader` enables memory-exhaustion denial of service

| Details             |                                                |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| Package             | `quick-xml`                      |
| Version             | `0.26.0`                   |
| URL                 | [https://github.com/tafia/quick-xml/issues/970](https://github.com/tafia/quick-xml/issues/970) |
| Date                | 2026-06-29                         |
| Patched versions    | `>=0.41.0`                  |

`NsReader` resolves namespaces by calling `NamespaceResolver::push` for every
`Start`/`Empty` event *before* the event is returned to the caller. `push`
iterated all `xmlns` / `xmlns:*` attributes on the start tag and, for each one,
appended the prefix bytes to an internal buffer and pushed a `NamespaceBinding`
(32 bytes on 64-bit) to an internal `Vec`, with no upper bound on the number of
declarations.

## Impact

A start tag with `N` namespace declarations drove roughly `3×` the tag's byte
size in `NamespaceResolver` heap, allocated *inside* `quick-xml` before the
`NsReader` consumer ever received the event and could inspect or reject it. A
consumer that bounds its *input* size therefore still cannot bound this
allocation: an `M`-byte start tag yields on the order of `3 × M` bytes of
resolver heap the caller never sees.

On untrusted XML this lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker force large heap
allocations with a single start tag. With several `NsReader`s running
concurrently on independent inputs (a common server pattern), the allocations
stack and can exhaust process memory, causing the operating system to kill the
process (OOM). This was confirmed against a real-world RPKI relying party (NLnet
Labs Routinator), where concurrent RRDP validation workers parsing a crafted
`snapshot.xml` exceeded the memory limit and the process was OOM-killed.

## Affected code paths

Consumers using `NsReader` (which always calls `NamespaceResolver::push` before
yielding `Start`/`Empty`), or calling `NamespaceResolver::push` directly. A plain
`Reader` that does not perform namespace resolution is not affected.

## Remediation

Upgrade to `quick-xml >= 0.41.0`. `NamespaceResolver::push` now rejects a start
tag that declares more than `DEFAULT_MAX_DECLARATIONS_PER_ELEMENT` (256)
namespace bindings, returning the new `NamespaceError::TooManyDeclarations`
instead of allocating without limit. The limit is configurable via
`NamespaceResolver::set_max_declarations_per_element` (use `usize::MAX` to
restore the previous unbounded behavior), and `NsReader::resolver_mut()` is
provided to reach it.

There is no clean workaround for `NsReader` consumers before 0.41.0, as the
allocation happens inside the reader with no configuration knob to cap it.

See [advisory page](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2026-0195.html) for additional details.

items.title: RUSTSEC-2026-0194: Quadratic run time when checking a start tag for duplicate attribute names
items.body:
> Quadratic run time when checking a start tag for duplicate attribute names

| Details             |                                                |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| Package             | `quick-xml`                      |
| Version             | `0.26.0`                   |
| URL                 | [https://github.com/tafia/quick-xml/issues/969](https://github.com/tafia/quick-xml/issues/969) |
| Date                | 2026-06-29                         |
| Patched versions    | `>=0.41.0`                  |

`BytesStart::attributes()` returns an `Attributes` iterator which, by default
(`with_checks(true)`), rejects a start tag that repeats an attribute name. For
each attribute yielded, the iterator compared the new name against every name
seen so far in the same tag using a linear scan, so a start tag with `N`
distinct attribute names cost `O(N²)` byte comparisons. There was no bound on
`N` other than the size of the buffered start tag.

## Impact

Any code that parses untrusted XML and iterates a start tag's attributes with
the default duplicate check enabled can be made to spend CPU time quadratic in
the number of attributes on a single tag. Because the check is pure computation
with no `.await`/I/O, an I/O-based timeout on the consumer (for example a read
or request timeout) cannot interrupt it while it runs.

Measured cost of a single start tag, release build:

| Attributes on one tag | Time |
|---|---|
| 80,000  | ~6 s   |
| 800,000 | ~10 min |

The cost grows with the square of the attribute count, so a start tag of a few
tens of megabytes can stall a parsing thread for hours. No memory is exhausted
and the parser does not crash; the effect is CPU exhaustion on the thread doing
the parsing: a single crafted start tag can pin a CPU core for minutes to hours,
denying service to that worker. A deployment that places a wall-clock bound on
parsing, or confines it to a non-critical thread, may consider the availability
impact lower.

## Affected code paths

* `BytesStart::attributes()` / `Attributes` iterated with checks enabled (the
  default), and `BytesStart::try_get_attribute`.
* `NsReader`, which resolves namespaces by iterating a tag's attributes and so
  reaches the same check internally.

Consumers that iterate attributes with `.attributes().with_checks(false)` and do
not use `NsReader` are not affected.

This was reported as reachable by a remote, unauthenticated attacker in a
real-world RPKI relying party (NLnet Labs Routinator) via a crafted RRDP
`snapshot.xml`.

## Remediation

Upgrade to `quick-xml >= 0.41.0`, where the duplicate check keeps the linear
scan for start tags with a small number of attributes and switches to an `O(1)`
hash pre-filter above a threshold, making the whole tag `O(N)`. The reported
`AttrError::Duplicated` positions are unchanged.

If upgrading is not possible and duplicate-name detection is not required,
disable it with `.attributes().with_checks(false)` (this does not help
`NsReader` consumers, which have no equivalent opt-out before 0.41.0).

See [advisory page](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2026-0194.html) for additional details.

items.title: Should `<Vec as Layer>::max_level_hint` be OFF when Vec is empty?
items.body:
## Bug Report

### Crates

* `tracing_subscriber`

### Version

* tracing-subscriber v0.3.23
* tracing-appender v0.2.5
* tracing v0.1.44
* tracing-core v0.1.36

### Platform

Linux 6.17.0

### The problem

Following (more or less) #2499, I added my own `Vec<Box<dyn Layer<..>>>` as a layer. The end result looks somewhat like that:

```rust
    let dyn_layers: Vec<Box<dyn Layer<...>>> = vec![];
    tracing_subscriber::registry()
        .with(dyn_layers)
        .with(env_filter_layer)
        .with(non_blocking_logger)
        .init();
```

I expected it to be the same as without the `.with(dyn_layers)`, instead, when adding `dyn_layers`, all other layers stopped working.

### The reason

I believe that's because  `<Vec as Layer>::max_level_hint` returns `LevelFilter::OFF` when the `Vec` is empty, which apparently turns of all events for all the other loggers (I'm not quite clear on the semantics of `.with`, I thought it shouldn't, even with `LevelFilter::OFF`)

### My Workaround

I initialize `dyn_layers` with a `Identity`, ensuring that it not toggle off log levels:

```rust
    let dyn_layers: Vec<Box<dyn Layer<...>>> = vec![Box::new(Identity::new()) as _];
    tracing_subscriber::registry()
        .with(dyn_layers)
        .with(env_filter_layer)
        .with(non_blocking_logger)
        .init();
```

### Context

My actual setup is more complex, plus I have a couple layers wrapped in a `reload::Layer`, but I don't think it should influence the result.

items.title: Opt-in compile-time check for duplicate field names in event!/span! macros?
items.body:
## Summary

Would the maintainers be open to an opt-in cargo feature (e.g. `strict-field-names`) that makes the `event!`, `span!`, `info!`, etc. macros fail to **compile** when the same field name appears more than once in a single call?

Asking before sending a PR to gauge interest.

## Current behavior

`tracing` today silently accepts duplicate field names in a single macro invocation. Reproducer:

```rust
info!(foo = 1, foo = 2);
info!(http.method = "GET", http.method = "POST");
```

Observed (verified against current `main`):

- `Event::metadata().fields().len() == 2` — both entries present in the `FieldSet`.
- The visitor receives two `record_*` calls, both with `Field::name() == "foo"` (different indices).
- `FieldSet::field("foo")` returns the first occurrence only (`position(|f| f == name)` in `tracing-core/src/field.rs`), so name-based lookup silently ignores the second.
- No warning, no diagnostic.

This is almost always a programmer mistake — the user typed the same key twice — and is currently invisible until it surfaces in a downstream subscriber (or doesn't, depending on the visitor).

## Proposal

A cargo feature on `tracing` (and matching support in `tracing-attributes` for `#[instrument(fields(...))]`) that, when enabled, emits a compile-time assertion alongside the existing callsite metadata, using a `const fn` over the `&'static str` field names already produced by `fieldset!`. MSRV-safe (`const` panic since 1.57). Off by default to preserve compatibility.

## Motivation

This came up while working on `opentelemetry-rust`, where the OpenTelemetry spec requires log/span attributes to be a map of unique keys. The SDK is debating whether to dedupe at runtime on the hot path (perf cost) or push the responsibility to producers. For the within-callsite case, a compile-time check in `tracing` would eliminate one whole class of duplicates at source. References: open-telemetry/opentelemetry-rust#3497, open-telemetry/opentelemetry-rust#3498.

## Question

Before writing a PR — is this something the maintainers would consider merging if implemented cleanly and gated behind an off-by-default feature? Or is the preference to keep this kind of check out of `tracing` core (e.g. leave it to a clippy lint or external proc-macro wrapper)?

Happy to send a draft PR if there's interest.

items.title: `#[instrument(err)]` can't produce a `&(dyn Error + 'static)` (for `tracing_opentelemetry`)
items.body:
## Feature Request

### Crates

- `tracing-attributes`

### Motivation

`#[instrument(err)]` logs the `error` field as either `Debug` or `Display`, but in order for [`tracing_opentelemetry::OpenTelemetryLayer::with_error_fields_to_exceptions`](https://docs.rs/tracing-opentelemetry/latest/tracing_opentelemetry/struct.OpenTelemetryLayer.html#method.with_error_fields_to_exceptions) to correctly set the `exception.message` and `exception.stacktrace` fields, the `error` field needs to be a `&(dyn Error + 'static)`.

Error return types are usually not a `&(dyn Error + 'static)`, so we need some way to transform the error type into that value, e.g. ([for `anyhow::Error`](https://docs.rs/anyhow/latest/anyhow/struct.Error.html#impl-AsRef%3Cdyn+Error+%2B+Send+%2B+Sync%3E-for-Error)) `AsRef::as_ref`. But this won't be the same for all types, so we should have some way of transforming the error before it's logged.

### Proposal

IMO this request is straightforward, and I'm interested in implementing it, but the syntax is the tricky part. I don't have strong opinions on the syntax here; see below for some options I've thought about.

### Alternatives

#### Closure

```rust
﻿#[instrument(err(|e| e.as_ref()))]
```

Here we let the user pass a _closure_ for transforming the error before it's logged. This doesn't hardcode any names, it's compatible with existing arguments, and makes the semantics clear.

#### Match-like

```rust
#[instrument(err(error => error.as_ref()))]
```

This says that we transform the `error` by calling `error.as_ref()` before returning it.

This syntax is a special duck; it isn't used anywhere else, and it doesn't match the form of other 'arguments' for this macro using parenthesis.

The `error =>` prefix could be mandatory, or it could be used to specify a name for the `Err` variable in the invocation (i.e. `err => err.as_ref()` could also be allowed).


#### Fields

```rust
#[instrument(err(fields(error = error.as_ref())))]
```

We could reuse the `fields` syntax for this, treating a field named `error` as a special value. This is hardcoded and kind of unintuitive; it doesn't work like plain `#[instrument(fields(...))]` does.

See:
- #3076

#### A new argument

```rust
#[instrument(err(value(err.as_ref())))]
```

Here, we hardcode a name (`err`) and let the user specify the `error` field's value with an expression.

This could be combined with the "match-like" syntax for more flexibility.

This syntax has the advantage of "looking like" the rest of the arguments and not introducing any new syntactic concepts.

items.title: tracing-subscriber module path matching
items.body:
## Feature Request

### Crates

tracing-subscriber

### Motivation

I am using multiple related crates which have the same prefix (specifically `tokio` and `tokio-xmpp`). While I do want log output from tokio, I want less of it than my default log level. For example:

```rs
let filter = filter::Targets::new()
    .with_default(LevelFilter::DEBUG)
    .with_target("tokio", LevelFilter::INFO);
``` 

This is currently possible by working around the prefix matching, but relatively annoying:

```rs
let filter = filter::Targets::new()
    .with_default(LevelFilter::DEBUG)
    .with_target("tokio_xmpp", LevelFilter::DEBUG)
    .with_target("tokio", LevelFilter::INFO);
``` 

### Proposal

The filter could have an additional way to add a filter which matches the module path instead of the string of the target or a configuration option to toggle this behavior per filter.

### Alternatives

The two alternatives are using:

1. in this case, `tokio::` as the target target
2. searching for all crates in the dependency tree which should have additional longs and manually using the longer prefix for them


Both of these options are slightly annoying when just wanting to filter a single crate.
